decks.domain: Scanning, space cushion, blind spots, entering traffic, signaling and passing

cards.front: How far ahead should you read the road, and why?
cards.back: Keep your eyes moving and read the road about one city block ahead, so you are not forced into last-minute decisions.

cards.front: How does the block-ahead rule differ from the following-distance count?
cards.back: Looking about one city block ahead is the scanning rule, and it is separate from the seconds-based count used for following distance.

cards.front: What should you do as you approach an intersection?
cards.back: As you approach an intersection, look both left and right before you continue.

cards.front: What does checking your rearview mirror often tell you?
cards.back: Checking the rearview mirror often shows you where traffic behind you is and warns you when someone is tailgating or closing in too fast.

cards.front: What two checks come before a lane change?
cards.back: Before a lane change, check the side mirrors and also turn your head to look over your shoulder.

cards.front: What lets you make decisions quickly and safely in traffic?
cards.back: When you keep track of how fast and where the traffic is in front, behind and on both sides, you can make decisions quickly and safely.

decks.domain: Scanning, space cushion, blind spots, entering traffic, signaling and passing

cards.front: How do you test whether you are following too closely?
cards.back: The manual's three-six second rule tests your gap: when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point such as a sign or overpass, start counting, and if you reach that point before you finish, you are following too closely.

cards.front: About how long does it take to count from one-thousand-one to one-thousand-four?
cards.back: Counting from one-thousand-one to one-thousand-four takes about four seconds.

cards.front: How does the four-second example count differ from the poor-conditions cushion?
cards.back: The count in the example runs to four and takes about four seconds, while the cushion the manual recommends in poor conditions spans three to six seconds.
cards.memory_hook: example four, cushion three to six

cards.front: How should your following distance change as your speed rises?
cards.back: The faster you go, the greater your following distance should be.

cards.front: How much cushion should you leave in poor road conditions?
cards.back: Poor road conditions call for more than a three-second cushion, so give yourself three to six seconds.

cards.front: Why does high speed shrink your margin for error?
cards.back: At high speed you travel farther while reacting to a problem, so your margin for error shrinks.

cards.front: What causes most rear-end crashes?
cards.back: Following too closely causes most rear-end crashes.

decks.domain: Scanning, space cushion, blind spots, entering traffic, signaling and passing

cards.front: Why does space around your vehicle matter, and where in the lane should you stay?
cards.back: Space around your vehicle gives you and other drivers time to react to emergencies, and staying in the middle of your lane helps create that cushion.

cards.front: How much room should you keep ahead of and behind your vehicle?
cards.back: Keep enough room ahead of you to stop suddenly, and enough room ahead and behind to pass or stop safely.

cards.front: How much room must you give a bicycle when you share a lane?
cards.back: When you share a lane with a bicycle, keep at least three feet between your vehicle and the rider and moderate your speed.

cards.front: How is following distance measured compared with bicycle clearance?
cards.back: Following distance is counted in seconds behind the vehicle ahead, while bicycle clearance in a shared lane is a fixed three feet to the side.

cards.front: How can you help the driver behind you keep a safe gap?
cards.back: You help the driver behind you keep a safe gap by holding a steady speed and signaling early before you slow down or stop.

cards.front: What should you do if someone is tailgating you?
cards.back: If someone is tailgating you, slow down gradually and open more space ahead, so you can brake more gently and give the tailgater time to react.

cards.front: What is the right response to a tailgater?
cards.back: A tailgater is handled by slowing gradually and adding space ahead of you, which lets you brake more gently when you must stop.

cards.front: What else can encourage a tailgater to go around you?
cards.back: When it is safe, changing to another lane encourages a tailgater to go around you.

cards.front: Whose safety do your actions affect when you stop suddenly?
cards.back: What you do affects the driver behind you, especially when you have to stop suddenly.

decks.domain: Scanning, space cushion, blind spots, entering traffic, signaling and passing

cards.front: What are blind spots?
cards.back: Blind spots are the areas at the left and right sides of your vehicle that your mirrors do not show.

cards.front: What should you do when parked cars or bushes block your view at an intersection?
cards.back: When cars parked near an intersection or bushes, trees or buildings block your view, creep forward slowly until you can see clearly, then go when the way is clear.

cards.front: How do you stay out of other drivers' blind spots?
cards.back: Stay out of other drivers' blind spots, watching for motorcycles too, by speeding up or dropping back rather than lingering beside them.

cards.front: Why should you not rely on your mirrors alone?
cards.back: Make sure other drivers can see your vehicle, and do not trust your mirrors alone to show vehicles or motorcycles beside you.

cards.front: What should you do to confirm the way is clear before changing lanes?
cards.back: Look over your shoulder to confirm the way is clear before changing lanes.

cards.front: How do you deal with your blind spots compared with other drivers' blind spots?
cards.back: Your own blind spots are cleared with a shoulder check, while other drivers' blind spots are avoided by speeding up or dropping back.

cards.front: What should you do when entering a road from a private drive?
cards.back: When entering the road from a side road or a private drive, stop and wait until traffic clears.

cards.front: Should you pull out because an oncoming vehicle has its turn signal on?
cards.back: Do not assume a vehicle or motorcycle with its turn signal on will really turn; wait until you see the driver commit to the turn before you pull out.

cards.front: Does another driver's blinking signal give you a gap to enter?
cards.back: Entering from a private drive means stopping and waiting for a clear gap, and another driver's blinking signal does not create that gap.

decks.domain: Scanning, space cushion, blind spots, entering traffic, signaling and passing

cards.front: When should you use your turn signals?
cards.back: Use your turn signals whenever you change direction, such as moving to another lane, turning at an intersection, merging onto a freeway, leaving a curb or pulling off the road.

cards.front: Why signal even when no one seems to be around?
cards.back: Signal out of habit even when no one else seems to be around, because the vehicle or motorcycle you have not noticed poses the greatest danger.

cards.front: What does communicating mean for a driver?
cards.back: Communicating means showing other drivers and pedestrians what you intend to do early enough to prevent a collision.

cards.front: How far before a turn should you signal?
cards.back: Signal at least one hundred feet, roughly four seconds, before you turn so others have time to react.

cards.front: About how many seconds of driving is the signaling distance?
cards.back: The turn-signal distance is one hundred feet, which the manual puts at about four seconds of driving.

cards.front: What does the law set for turns and signaling?
cards.back: The law sets the lanes and positions you must use for turns and requires a signal at least one hundred feet before you turn.

cards.front: When should you signal for a turn that comes just past an intersection?
cards.back: If your turn comes just past an intersection, wait until you are inside the intersection to signal, because drivers there could pull into your path.

cards.front: How does signaling for a turn just past an intersection break the usual rule?
cards.back: For a turn just past an intersection you hold the signal until you are inside the intersection, the opposite of the usual rule to signal well ahead.

cards.front: What should you check after finishing a turn or lane change?
cards.back: After you finish your move, make sure the turn signal has gone off.

cards.front: Does signaling give you the right-of-way?
cards.back: A signal warns others of your move and gives them time to react, but it does not give you the right-of-way.

cards.front: What ways may you use to show a turn?
cards.back: You may show a turn with your turn signals, with hand signals, or with both.

cards.front: Which moves always call for a signal?
cards.back: Always signal before changing lanes, turning at an intersection or into a driveway or alley, entering or leaving a freeway, pulling away from the curb, or pulling over to the side of the road.

cards.front: When using hand signals, what else must you signal?
cards.back: When you are using hand signals, also signal before you slow down or stop suddenly.

cards.front: What extra case do hand signals cover?
cards.back: Hand signals add one case the turn-signal list does not: signaling before you slow down or stop suddenly.

decks.domain: Scanning, space cushion, blind spots, entering traffic, signaling and passing

cards.front: How do you pass a vehicle going your way?
cards.back: To pass a vehicle or motorcycle going your way, signal the lane change and pass on the left.

cards.front: What must you be sure of before passing?
cards.back: Before passing, be sure you have the time and room to get completely ahead of the other vehicle without endangering oncoming traffic.

cards.front: When may you return to the right lane after passing?
cards.back: Return to the right lane once you can see the whole front, or both headlights, of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror, after a shoulder check and a signal.

cards.front: What cue tells you it is safe to return after passing?
cards.back: The cue for returning to the right lane is seeing the whole front or both headlights of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.

cards.front: Do the passing steps change for slow motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds?
cards.back: The same passing steps apply when you pass slow-moving motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds.

cards.front: What should you do when a vehicle behind you wants to pass?
cards.back: If a vehicle behind you honks or flashes its lights to pass, move right when it is safe and let it by, and never speed up while you are being passed.

cards.front: What must you never do while being passed?
cards.back: Being passed calls for moving right when it is safe and letting the other vehicle by; speeding up while being passed is never allowed.

cards.front: When may you pass on the right?
cards.back: Passing on the right is permitted only when safe and either the driver ahead is turning left, you are on an open highway clearly marked for two or more lanes in your direction, or you are in a business or residential district marked for two or more lanes in your direction; never leave the paved or main roadway to pass on the right, and never pass to the left of a driver signaling a left turn.

cards.front: Where else may you pass on the right?
cards.back: Passing on the right is also allowed on an open highway clearly marked for two or more lanes moving in your direction.

cards.front: When is passing on the right allowed instead of the left?
cards.back: Normal passing is on the left; passing on the right needs both safety and a listed condition such as a driver ahead who is turning left.

recap_hooks.text: Look a block ahead, check left and right at intersections, and use mirrors and a shoulder check before changing lanes.
Count from a fixed point to test your gap, and add more distance at higher speed and in poor conditions.
Keep space all around, give a bicycle three feet, and slow gradually for a tailgater.
Shoulder-check your own blind spots, stay out of others', and never pull out on a turn signal alone.
Signal every move about one hundred feet ahead, but remember that a signal never gives you the right-of-way.
Pass on the left with time and room, return when both headlights show in your mirror, and never speed up while being passed.
